abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a multi-layer network paradigm for modeling heterogeneous interactions in urban transportation systems, fundamentally reconceptualizing how traffic flow dynamics emerge from coupled infrastructure layers. Traditional traffic models treat transportation networks as monolithic structures, failing to capture the complex interdependencies between road infrastructure, public transit systems, and emerging mobility-on-demand services. Our proposed framework employs complex network theory to characterize topological properties across layers while incorporating dynamic coupling mechanisms that capture travelers' mode-switching behaviors. We develop analytical expressions for cross-layer traffic propagation under various demand scenarios and validate theoretical predictions against empirical data from three metropolitan areas. The paradigm shift lies in treating transportation networks as multiplex systems where identical nodes participate in different layers simultaneously, enabling analysis of how disruptions in one layer cascade through the entire mobility ecosystem. Results demonstrate that this approach provides superior predictive accuracy for congestion formation compared to single-layer models, with up to 34% improvement in高峰期 demand prediction. This framework establishes a new theoretical foundation for smart mobility research and offers actionable insights for transportation network design in smart cities.

This paper presents a theoretically grounded approach to traffic speed prediction that significantly advances the state-of-the-art by integrating physics-informed neural networks with classical traffic flow theory. Existing data-driven methods treat traffic dynamics as black-box functions, neglecting fundamental physical constraints that govern vehicular movement. We address this limitation by embedding partial differential equations derived from Lighthill-Whitham-Richards traffic flow theory into the neural network architecture, ensuring predictions remain consistent with hydrodynamic traffic models. The proposed physics-informed framework enables accurate short-term prediction under both free-flow and congested conditions without requiring prohibitively large training datasets. We derive theoretical bounds on prediction error and prove convergence properties under standard traffic demand assumptions. Extensive validation using loop detector data from urban arterials demonstrates 23% mean absolute error reduction compared to pure machine learning approaches. The theoretical framework further reveals that incorporating traffic control constraints improves prediction stability during phase transitions. This work provides rigorous analytical foundations for deploying machine learning in traffic management systems while maintaining physical interpretability essential for transportation network operations.

We present a distributed edge computing architecture for vehicle-to-everything communication that fundamentally reimagines intelligent transportation infrastructure for the era of autonomous vehicles. Current centralized V2X architectures introduce prohibitive latency for safety-critical applications and cannot scale with increasing vehicle density in urban environments. Our proposed paradigm employs a hierarchical edge computing framework where computational resources are distributed across roadside units, mobile edge servers, and vehicle onboard systems, enabling real-time processing of safety messages with sub-10ms latency. The architecture introduces novel consensus mechanisms for distributed intersection management where no central controller exists, allowing autonomous vehicles to coordinate crossing sequences through Byzantine-fault-tolerant protocols. We implement a full prototype using software-defined radio and mobile edge computing platforms, demonstrating practical feasibility through field tests in a controlled test track environment. System evaluation reveals 47% reduction in communication latency compared to cloud-based approaches while maintaining 99.999% reliability for safety-critical messages. This paradigm shift from centralized to distributed intelligent infrastructure addresses fundamental scalability limitations and enables new applications in autonomous vehicle coordination, transforming how smart cities approach transportation AI deployment.

This paper presents an adaptive traffic signal control system that substantially improves urban intersection efficiency through integration of reinforcement learning with connected vehicle data streams. Prior adaptive signal systems rely on aggregate detector measurements, providing incomplete visibility into approaching traffic composition and trajectories. Our designed system processes high-frequency vehicle trajectory data from vehicle-to-infrastructure communication to predict queue formation and optimize phase sequences proactively rather than reactively. We develop a novel reward shaping mechanism that balances intersection throughput against network-wide coordination objectives, preventing myopic optimization that degrades arterial performance. The implementation incorporates a modular software architecture supporting heterogeneous intersection configurations and integrates with existing traffic management centers through standard protocols. Deployment across twelve intersections in a mid-sized city demonstrated 18% reduction in average vehicle delay and 12% improvement in throughput during peak periods. The system gracefully handles mixed traffic containing both connected and conventional vehicles by calibrating predictions using historical detector data. This work provides a scalable pathway for modernizing traffic control infrastructure in smart cities, delivering immediate operational benefits while establishing foundations for full autonomous vehicle integration.
